scenes.name: 1966: el año del single
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El libro son doce ensayos, uno por mes, cada uno a partir de un single. 1966 fue el último año en que el 45 fue la forma principal del pop, antes de que Sgt. Pepper’s convirtiera el LP en la fuerza creativa y comercial en el verano de 1967: en dos o tres minutos cabían ideas, actitudes, letras y experimentos que después se estirarían en álbumes de cuarenta minutos. El pop dejó de ser comercio, romance adolescente o diversión para volverse una experiencia total, «la única cosa viva» según Lou Reed, y el prisma con el que se interpretaba el mundo. El año empezó en el pop y acabó en el rock; empezó en la Gran Sociedad de Johnson y acabó con el resurgir republicano. Hubo ambición, aceleración y compresión, y una reacción proporcional de quienes veían que todo cambiaba demasiado deprisa. Savage, que cumplió trece años ese verano escuchando Radio Caroline South, se ciñe a los singles, sobre todo los que entraron en las listas de Billboard y Record Retailer, y deja fuera el free jazz, el minimalismo, el ska, los happenings y los situacionistas.

scenes.name: Warhol, la Factory y el pop de 1966
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En la primavera de 1966 Warhol era el artista más famoso de Estados Unidos y ya no hacía arte en el sentido tradicional: había anunciado en 1965 que dejaba la pintura por el cine, la gente y los entornos totales. La Factory de la calle 47 Este era a la vez cadena de producción de serigrafías, plató y escenario abierto; un espejo de la sociedad neoyorquina donde lo que esta despreciaba (drag queens, yonquis, chaperos, perturbados) podía volverse superstar. Sus cuadros devolvían a América sus valores (sexo, muerte, crimen, fama, dinero, producción en masa) y sus series de desastres el regodeo mediático en la muerte. Obrero gay de Pittsburgh con una rabia de outsider, se convirtió en estrella de rock en el caos de su retrospectiva de Filadelfia (octubre de 1965). Gloria Steinem lo puso en el centro de la cultura pop en Life y Susan Sontag hizo de lo camp una obsesión; Batman, A Clockwork Orange, el caso de los asesinatos de Tucson y Capote alimentaban el aire de violencia que él recortaba de las revistas. Con la anfetamina el ambiente se volvió paranoico y cruel; Danny Williams, su amante y autor de las luces del EPI, desapareció en julio. Durante 1966, sin pretenderlo, «se convirtió en América».
scenes.family: Vanguardia: Warhol, Velvet, free jazz, arte

scenes.name: Downtown: graffiti, punk y hip hop en el Mudd Club, Negril y el Roxy
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Fab 5 Freddy (Fred Brathwaite), del grupo de grafiteros de Brooklyn Fabulous 5 con Lee Quiñones, ofrecía en The Village Voice murales por encargo; con Michael Holman montó la Canal Zone Party (1979), donde apareció Jean-Michel Basquiat, mitad de SAMO, y llevó a Bambaataa al Mudd Club. La Zulu Nation y los Funky 4 + 1, que mezclaban punk y hip hop ante los Beastie Boys, bajaron al Ritz, el Mudd Club, Danceteria, Negril y el Roxy de Kool Lady Blue: en Negril, cedido por el mánager de los Clash, se juntaron por primera vez los cuatro elementos; en el Roxy, una pista de patinaje de la calle 18, Bambaataa, Afrika Islam y Grand Mixer D.ST pinchaban para Bianca Jagger, Warhol, la Rock Steady Crew o Madonna. Debbie Harry y Chris Stein (Blondie), amigos de Flash, nombraron a Freddy y a Flash en «Rapture» (1981), primer rap número 1 en Billboard, y llevaron a los Funky 4 + 1 a Saturday Night Live (14 de febrero de 1981), primera actuación de hip hop en la televisión nacional. Para Holman, sin el abrazo del downtown el hip hop no habría sido lo que fue; para Dante Ross, los negros se llevaron pantalones pitillo y opiáceos y los blancos toda esa cultura.

podcast.title: Album Cover Design & Peelable Banana
podcast.body: Andy Warhol designed the iconic album cover for "The Velvet Underground & Nico," famously insisting on a peelable banana sticker. This creative decision led to significant production challenges and delays, making the album costly and complex to manufacture, but Warhol refused to allow its release without this specific artistic element. "Andy Warhol había diseñado la portada, pero está posicionado con que el plátano de la portada fuese una pegatina que se pudiese quitar."

podcast.title: Circle of Friends and "Walk on the Wild Side"
podcast.body: Lou Reed's hit song "Walk on the Wild Side" tells the true stories of several figures within Andy Warhol's social circle. These individuals included Holly Woodlawn, a transsexual from Miami; Candy Darling, another transsexual; and Joe Campbell, who was referred to as the "Sugar Plum Fairy." "This song told the true story of a number of people in Andy Warhol's circle."

podcast.title: Influence on Lou Reed's "Transformer"
podcast.body: Lou Reed's experiences at Andy Warhol's Factory heavily influenced the thematic content of his "Transformer" album. The record delves into "macabre stories" from the Factory, and his song "Walk on the Wild Side" specifically references and lists many notable characters from that environment. "Y realmente la temática del Transformer viene a ser no solo esas grabaciones desechadas de la parte de la Belbet Underground sino las experiencias que el propio Luric había tenido en la factoria de Andy Warhol."

podcast.title: Insistence on Nico Joining The Velvet Underground
podcast.body: Andy Warhol introduced Nico, a German actress and model from The Factory, to The Velvet Underground. He felt the band needed a "beautiful woman" and was obsessed with Nico at the time, thereby forcing her into the band against the opinions of John Cale and Lou Reed. "Andy Warhol le parecía que hacía falta una mujer guapa dentro de la velvita underground. Entonces para él la idea perfecta era Nico en ese tiempo estaba sesionado con ella y entonces pues la introduce un poco con calzador en contra de la opinión de John Kale y de Lou Reed."

podcast.title: Lou Reed's Hatred After Velvet Underground
podcast.body: After the dissolution of the Velvet Underground, Lou Reed developed a "true hatred" for Andy Warhol. This animosity might have contributed to the somewhat negative portrayal of Factory characters and their "bad influence" or "bad lives" in Lou Reed's work, such as the song "Walk on the Wild Side." "Aquí de hecho también puede que tengamos un poco de rencor hacia la mala relación que quedó del Luric con el propio Andy Warhol que quedaron como muy enemistados con Luric, sintiendo un verdadero odio hacia Andy Warhol, justo tras la disolución de la Belbet Underground."

podcast.title: MGM Executive's Reaction to Album
podcast.body: After hearing "The Velvet Underground & Nico," a Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer executive famously told Andy Warhol, "Andy, esto es una mierda" ("Andy, this is shit"). Ironically, this same individual was responsible for the Verve Records division and ultimately oversaw the album's release. "un director, un director ejecutivo de la Metro Golden Mayor después de escucharlo, le decía Andy Warhol la famosa frase de Andy, esto es una mierda."

podcast.body: Andy Warhol commissioned three songs for a Broadway musical he was attempting to stage. These songs later appeared on Lou Reed's 1972 album *Transformer*, indicating Warhol's influence on Reed's creative output. "Three of the songs were commissioned by Andy Warhol for a Broadway musical he was trying to stage."

podcast.title: Reaction to Being Fired
podcast.body: According to John Cale, while Andy Warhol initially claimed to take his dismissal well after Lou Reed fired him, he directly called Lou Reed a "dirty rat" and never spoke to him again, indicating a very sour end to their relationship. "Andy Warhol se lo tomó muy bien pero que, de girectamente, le dijo a Lurri que era una sucia rata y nunca más le volvió a hablar."

xref.title: Discovery and Patronage by Andy Warhol (December 1965)
xref.body: One night, just as The Velvet Underground faced a second firing from Cafe Bizarre, Andy Warhol and his entourage, including groupies and "weirdos," unexpectedly visited the club. Warhol was so profoundly impressed by their "avant-garde approach to rock" that he immediately signed them to be his official house band at his performance art headquarters, The Factory, located on East 47th Street. Warhol assumed the roles of their patron, producer, and promoter, a pivotal moment that launched the band's "long, strange road to becoming legends as the first alternative rock band in history." "Andy Warhol adopts the Velvet Underground, thereby giving the band the break they needed, to eventually be hailed as the founders of alternative rock"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7

xref.title: Early Lo-Fi Aesthetic (1966-1967)
xref.body: The band, composed of broke musicians associated with Andy Warhol, aimed to make a record with a meager budget of possibly $1,500. Their debut album, released in March 1967, was characterized by significant hiss, distortion, recording errors, a rough final mix, and poor stereo imaging, with singer Nico often being off-key. Despite these technical flaws, the primitive sound contributed to its appeal for a segment of music fans who valued authenticity and rebellion. "The Velvet Underground's records were generally derided for sounding bad, which made all kind of sense in the late 1960s and the early 1970s because the goal back then was to achieve perfect sound or something close to it."

xref.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
xref.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. "The Ramones played their first ever show at a New York club called CBGB."

xref.title: Andy Warhol's Death as Catalyst for Partial Reunion (1987)
xref.body: The death of their former mentor, patron, and producer, Andy Warhol, on February 22, 1987, after routine gallbladder surgery, prompted Lou Reed and John Cale to re-evaluate their relationship and record a tribute album, "Songs for Drella." "That's when their former mentor, patron and producer Andy Warhol died after routine surgery on his gallbladder. The death of a friend and colleague will make anyone reevaluate things."

xref.title: Full Reunion Concert in Edinburgh (1993)
xref.body: The combination of Andy Warhol's death, the recognition by Václav Havel and the "Velvet Revolution," and the increasing mythology built by reissued records finally pushed the band to reunite, with their first reunion concert taking place in Edinburgh, Scotland, on June 1, 1993. "The Velvet Underground reunion began with a concert in Edinburgh, Scotland on June 1st 1993."

xref.title: Andy Warhol's Influence and Management
xref.body: The band was an integral part of Andy Warhol's "freaky New York crowd," and Warhol, who served as their manager and producer, encouraged them to continuously improvise and experiment, regardless of prevailing musical trends. "They were part of Andy Warhol's freaky New York crowd, and he encouraged them to continue to improvise and experiment, regardless of what everyone else was doing."

xref.title: Andy Warhol's Producer Credit
xref.body: Andy Warhol was credited as the producer for the band's 1967 debut record. However, he admitted to not knowing much about making records, and his role was primarily to inspire and encourage the band, not to handle any technical aspects of production. "Okay, he was credited as being the producer but he didn't really know much about making records. He was just there to inspire and encourage them. He didn't touch anything."

xref.body: During Weezer's hiatus after "Make Believe," drummer Patrick Wilson and bassist Scott Shriner worked on a group called The Relationship. Brian Bell pursued his side project, The Special Goodness. Pat and Brian also ventured into acting in a film called "Factory Girl," with Pat playing John Cale of The Velvet Underground and Brian portraying Andy Warhol. "drummer Patrick Wilson and bass player Scott Schreiner went to work on a group called The Relationship."

xref.title: Family Background and Influences
xref.body: Florence's father, Nick, was an "old punk" who had associations with Joe Strummer before The Clash formed, and later became an ad executive for Aero Chocolate Bars, resembling Andy Warhol. Her paternal grandfather hung out with the Warhol crowd at Studio 54, and another grandfather, a deputy editor of the Daily Telegraph, gave her the soundtrack to *The Rocky Horror Picture Show*, which became her first favorite record and sparked a crush on its creator, Richard O'Brien, at age 10. "And then there's her father, Nick. He was an old punk who once hung out with Joe Strummer in the days before he joined the clash."

xref.title: Mentorship by Andy Warhol
xref.body: Andy Warhol, the pop artist, heard The Velvet Underground at The Cafe Bizarre and immediately brought them into his circle. He hired them to perform at the "freaky parties" held at The Factory, his New York headquarters, becoming their mentor and chief patron. "And one guy who heard about their raw and gritty approach was Andy Warhol."

xref.title: Nico's Inclusion for Visual Interest
xref.body: Andy Warhol encouraged the band to include German model Nico, primarily for visual interest, as part of their presentation. "Warhol became The Velvet's mentor and chief patron, encouraging them to hire on a German model named Nico for visual interest."

xref.title: Pioneering Alternative Status
xref.body: Some people insist The Velvet Underground was the first true alternative group in history due to their radical sound and themes which diverged significantly from the mainstream rock and roll of the era. Their music, which was "too weird for the mainstream," necessitated a partnership with an independent label that was willing to experiment. "This isn't the Velvet Underground. The Velvet Underground from their 1967 debut album, which was released on Verve, an independent jazz label founded in 1956, that decided to take a chance on the Velvet's, thanks largely to the group's connection to Andy Warhol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
xref.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. "Bowie immersed himself into this new persona, this doomed pansexual alien, and he invented a new name for himself. It was Ziggy Stardust."
